title: Choose sampling, evidence assembly, citations, and output constraints so a generated result can be checked and safely consumed by the next component

questions.prompt:
A pipeline sends supplier contracts to an LLM and writes its output straight into a billing system. The request uses constrained decoding (a provider-enforced JSON schema), with fields `renewal_date` and `notice_period_days`. Every completed response parses and passes schema validation. An audit finds that some records still have a wrong `renewal_date`: the value is a real date from the contract, but it is the signing date.

Which change most directly stops these wrong values reaching the billing system?
options: Set `temperature` to 0 so the model always picks its most likely date, which removes the wrong-date errors.
Require each field to cite its source text, then check after generation that the cited text supports the value before writing it.
Switch from constrained decoding to JSON mode so the model has more freedom to choose the correct date field.
Raise `max_completion_tokens` so the model has room to read the whole contract before it fills in the date field.

rubric.point: Chooses the post-generation evidence check: the schema proves shape, not meaning, so the field value must be checked against its cited source before it is used.

questions.model:
**B.** Schema enforcement only guarantees valid shape; a well-formed date can still be the wrong one. Linking each field to its source text and checking that the source supports the value catches semantic errors before the billing system consumes them.

*Why not the others:* temperature 0 makes the choice more deterministic but can repeat the same wrong date; JSON mode is looser and still checks no meaning; the output limit does not control how much input the model reads, and these responses were not truncated.

questions.prompt:
A RAG system retrieves 12 complete document chunks, already ranked by relevance. The prompt budget left for evidence fits only about 5 complete chunks. One engineer suggests cutting every chunk down to its first few lines so that all 12 fit.

How should the system fit the retrieved evidence into this budget, and why?

rubric.point: Method: keeps the highest-ranked chunks complete (about 5) and drops the lower-ranked ones, rather than truncating every chunk. Mentioning that the most relevant chunks go first is fine but not required.
Reason: truncated fragments can lose the content that supports or explains a claim and add noise, so a few complete, high-quality chunks ground and cite answers better than many partial ones.

questions.model: Keep the top ~5 ranked chunks whole and drop the lower-ranked ones, instead of cutting every chunk down. Cut-down fragments can lose the part that actually supports a claim and add noise, so a few complete chunks ground and cite the answer better than 12 partial ones.
